title: ASOF JOIN memory usage
body:
### What happens?

DuckDB runs out of memory while executing `ASOF JOIN` query in `select_binance_transaction_times_and_prices.sql`.

(Please extract source files from [binance_duckdb_asof_join.zip](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/files/12062409/binance_duckdb_asof_join.zip).)

```
$ unzip -l binance_duckdb_asof_join.zip
Archive:  binance_duckdb_asof_join.zip
  Length      Date    Time    Name
---------  ---------- -----   ----
     1043  2023-07-15 13:02   get_binance_trades_to_parquet
      766  2023-07-15 13:10   import_trades_from_parquet.py
      245  2023-07-15 13:21   select_binance_transaction_times_and_prices.sql
      537  2023-07-15 13:19   transaction_times.csv
---------                     -------
     2591                     4 files
```

### To Reproduce

1. Download price history data files for coin pair BTCUSDT:
    ```
    for month in $(seq 1 12)
    do
      # Note: requires bash, duckdb, wget, and GNU zcat.
      ./get_binance_trades_to_parquet BTCUSDT 2022 $month
    done
    ```
1. Import price history for coin pair BTCUSDT into DuckDB database `binance.duckdb`:
    ```
    for month in $(seq 1 12)
    do
      python import_trades_from_parquet.py BTCUSDT 2022 $month
    done
    ```
1. Execute `ASOF JOIN` query:
    ```
    cat select_binance_transaction_times_and_prices.sql | duckdb binance.duckdb
    ```

### OS:

Ubuntu Server 22.04

### DuckDB Version:

v0.8.2-dev1764 07b0b0a2a4

### DuckDB Client:

CLI

### Full Name:

Derek Mahar

### Affiliation:

Self-employed

### Have you tried this on the latest `master` branch?

- [X] I agree

### Have you tried the steps to reproduce? Do they include all relevant data and configuration? Does the issue you report still appear there?

- [X] I agree

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Script `get_binance_trades_to_parquet` requires GNU zcat in order to extract the single CSV file from the zip archive and write it to standard output.  I have GNU zcat 1.10 in Ubuntu Server 22.04.2:

```
$ zcat --version
zcat (gzip) 1.10
Copyright (C) 2007, 2011-2018 Free Software Foundation, Inc.
This is free software.  You may redistribute copies of it under the terms of
the GNU General Public License <https://www.gnu.org/licenses/gpl.html>.
There is NO WARRANTY, to the extent permitted by law.

Written by Paul Eggert.
```

My guess is that Apple gzip isn't equivalent to GNU zcat.

Alternatively, if you have BusyBox, temporarily alias `zcat` to `busybox unzip -p`, which in this case behaves the same, or edit script `get_binance_trades_to_parquet` and replace `zcat` with `busybox unzip -p`.  If you have neither of these, but have `unzip`, in `get_binance_trades_to_parquet`, replace

```
wget $wget_options $file_url |
  zcat - |
  duckdb -c "$copy_sql"
```

with

```
wget --quiet $file_url
unzip -p $coin_pair-trades-$year-$month.zip | duckdb -c "$copy_sql"
```

This will leave both the source zip file and the target Parquet file on your disk, so make sure you have enough disk space to store both.

comments.body:
OK I finally got the test data built, and according to `top` the peak memory usage is around 30GB. Not great, but also not huge. IF this is more memory than you have available, have you tried using `SET external=True` and setting up a temporary directory?

I am rather appalled by the performance, however:

```
Run Time (s): real 1175.622 user 1713.975005 sys 10745.660641
```

That seems excessive for sorting two columns in a 1.2GR table and making 21 ordered probes into it.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
Yes you need a temporary directory if you are running out of memory:

```sql
PRAGMA temp_directory='path/to/temp/dir';
```

I did some crude profiling and found that almost all the time (15 minutes) is spent sorting, which seems wrong, so there may be an issue with how AsOf and Window handle sorting without partitioning.

comments.body:
> What do you mean by "without partitioning"?

Just that there are no equality conditions. (It's the same code that windowing uses, so sometimes I get the terminology mixed up!) I think the current code creates one partition and sorts it instead of just sorting.

According to the DuckDB documentation, PRAGMA [`temp_directory`](https://duckdb.org/docs/sql/pragmas#temp-directory-for-spilling-data-to-disk--defaults-to-tmp) defaults to `.tmp`.  When I run `cat select_binance_transaction_times_and_prices.sql | duckdb binance.duckdb`, DuckDB creates a directory called `binance.duckdb.tmp`, fills it with many large files, but still runs out of memory and dies.  The virtual machine in which I run the query has 16 GB of memory.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
This query does require a huge amount of memory right now. When I run it without limited memory it gets up to about 90GB before dying. But I can limit the memory to about 30GB with paging and it takes around 15 minutes to finish.

It does seem to me that for your situation writing your own join is far more tractable, and we should consider trying to detect it. But as far as I can tell from profiling, all that is happening is we are just sorting the uncompressed data and it takes a lot of memory (either RAM or disk) to do that.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body: Would it be reasonable to require that the right hand table be sorted?  The [ASOF JOIN](https://clickhouse.com/docs/en/sql-reference/statements/select/join#asof-join-usage) operation in Clickhouse makes this assumption.  In this case, the price table is sorted in ascending order by time stamp.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
Unfortunately, we actually don't know that! We are planning to detect and leverage ordering metadata but not yet.

When we get that, we could just have the planner notice that the incoming relation is ordered and use a different physical operator and fall back to the current approach when we need to sort. Then you get the best of both worlds.

I do think there are still some things we can do in your situation because the problem is that your data gets highly compressed (lots of proximity in prices and timestamps) but we uncompress it and copy it and sort it. There is no reason we can't avoid one of the copies and we have work underway to compress intermediate results. Still not as good as knowing the data is already ordered, but it would at least complete.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body: @reporter I have another change that reduces the memory for your query to about 52GB by avoiding unnecessary partitioning. One thing I notice is that you are representing the prices as doubles, when it looks like they would fit in a `DECIMAL(7,2)`, which is under 32 bits wide. If so, that would reduce the memory requirements by 25%.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
I deleted my previous comment because it was incorrect.

After changing the data type of price from `DOUBLE` to `DECIMAL(10,2)`, qty from `DOUBLE` to `DECIMAL(12,8)`, and quote_qty from `DOUBLE` to `DECIMAL(16,8)`, I observed that the size of `binance.duckdb` dropped by about 25%.  (I chose a decimal precision of 10 for the price in order to accommodate a relatively large future increase in the Bitcoin price.)

Unfortunately, DuckDB runs out of disk space on my machine when it attempts to run the `ASOF JOIN`.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
I just tried a rewrite using `arg_max ` and it ran quickly (32s) in about 8GB of RAM:

```sql
CREATE TEMP TABLE transation_times AS
	FROM "fnord.csv";

WITH prices AS (
	SELECT
		time,
		price 
	FROM trades_btcusdt
), candidates AS (
	SELECT
	  UTC_Time,
	  p.time,
	  p.price
	FROM transation_times t INNER JOIN prices p
	  ON t.UTC_Time >= p.time
	WHERE t.UTC_Time >= '2022-01-01'
	  AND t.UTC_Time < '2023-01-01'
)
SELECT UTC_Time, arg_max(price, time) AS price
FROM candidates
GROUP BY ALL
ORDER BY ALL;
```

The reason this is so effective is that it converts the join into a nested loop join with the small table on the inside. 

```   
┌───────────────────────────┐                             
│       HASH_GROUP_BY       │                             
│   ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─   │                             
│             #0            │                             
│      arg_max(#1, #2)      │                             
└─────────────┬─────────────┘                                                          
┌─────────────┴─────────────┐                             
│         PROJECTION        │                             
│   ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─   │                             
│          UTC_Time         │                             
│           price           │                             
│            time           │                             
└─────────────┬─────────────┘                                                          
┌─────────────┴─────────────┐                             
│         PROJECTION        │                             
│   ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─   │                             
│          UTC_Time         │                             
│            time           │                             
│           price           │                             
└─────────────┬─────────────┘                                                          
┌─────────────┴─────────────┐                             
│      NESTED_LOOP_JOIN     │                             
│   ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─   │                             
│           INNER           │                             
│      time <= UTC_Time     ├──────────────┐              
│   ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─   │              │              
│           EC: 32          │              │              
└─────────────┬─────────────┘              │                                           
┌─────────────┴─────────────┐┌─────────────┴─────────────┐
│         SEQ_SCAN          ││         SEQ_SCAN          │
│   ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─   ││   ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─   │
│       trades_btcusdt      ││      transation_times     │
│   ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─   ││   ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─   │
│            time           ││          UTC_Time         │
│           price           ││   ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─   │
│   ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─   ││ Filters: UTC_Time>=2022-01│
│       EC: 1200493891      ││ -01 00:00:00 AND UTC_Time │
│                           ││  <2023-01-01 00:00:00 AND │
│                           ││    UTC_Time IS NOT NULL   │
│                           ││   ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─   │
│                           ││           EC: 4           │
└───────────────────────────┘└───────────────────────────┘                             
```
So essentially it just scans the price table and emits candidate matches for each "probe" row, and the aggregate only keeps the best one so far. The "build" scan and aggregation is then completely parallelisable and runs on all my cores.

The one caveat is that you have to import the `csv` into a temp table so that the optimiser can use the row count statistics  to orient the join.

This is an interesting rewrite idea for the planner and I'll think about it some more.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body: Thought about this some more and you can only do this if the only fields from the probe side are join keys. But still seems useful. And if you have equality keys you can use a hash join with a predicate.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
@participant1, your [solution using `arg_max`](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/issues/8265#issuecomment-1856380441) ran in just under 21 s in an Ubuntu 24.04 virtual machine on my Minisforum UM690 running a Ryzen 9 6900HX.

Your `arg_max` query seems similar to one that I found that uses a [lateral join](https://github.com/timescale/timescaledb-toolkit/issues/162#issuecomment-865216150) to compute an ASOF join in TimescaleDB.  Running an adapted version of my ASOF join query that instead uses a lateral join, DuckDB v1.1.2-dev38 (45559f5eeb) unfortunately runs out of temporary disk space "memory".

In case you are curious, here is the lateral join query that I executed in DuckDB:

```
WITH prices AS (
  SELECT
    time,
    price
  FROM trades_btcusdt
)
SELECT
  UTC_Time,
  p.price
FROM "transaction_times.csv" t,
  LATERAL (
    SELECT price
    FROM prices p
    WHERE p.time <= t.UTC_Time
    ORDER BY p.time DESC
    LIMIT 1
  ) p
WHERE t.UTC_Time >= '2022-01-01'
  AND t.UTC_Time < '2023-01-01'
;
```

So far, ClickHouse is the only database that I've used that has successfully completed my ASOF join query.

I have implemented the alternate plan for small probe tables on `main`, so please grab the latest build and see if it works for you. 

There will also be a blog post on this coming out shortly explaining what I did, and the cutoff for the alternate plan is when the probe table is somewhere around 32-64 rows (you have 21). In the future we hope to be able to leverage existing ordering metadata to improve the build process, but that will not be soon.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
The improvement I made was to plan a nested loop join when the probe table is small. Unfortunately, that is a quadratic operation, so it gets Really Bad after the probe side gets above 40 rows or so. I wrote a [blog post](https://duckdb.org/2025/02/19/asof-plans.html) on the whole saga if you want the gory details. But it's pretty clear from the measurements that 240 rows is way above the performance cutoff.

Most of the memory is spent sorting the data and we have improvements to the sort code coming.  There is also an issue related to some scheduling work I did on the window operator where we are not using multiple cores for a single partition/equality condition. This is especially bad for AsOf when there is only an inequality (like windowing without partitions). Fixing this will not improve the sort memory footprint but should allow greater parallelisation of the probe phase.  Even better, the two changes will interact because the new sort code should allow me to scan the sorted data at a much finer granularity, enabling higher parallelism.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Would it not improve query performance considerably if the query command could inform the query planner that the right-hand side table (the "lookup" or "reference" table) is already sorted so that the planner could skip the sorting operation?

This scenario would be common in time series cases like mine where the events in the reference table are historical or archival, will never change, and might already be sorted by timestamp (perhaps "frozen" in read-only Parquet files) or must be sorted only once.  This scenario further assumes that any new events added to the time series archive (for example, in new Parquet files for subsequent periods) are all greater in time than earlier events already in the archive and are in ascending time order.  (In this scenario, it would be useful if one could also specify in the query the order in which the query planner should read the input Parquet files.)

comments.author: participant1
comments.body: I think you are suggesting a "hint"? We don't currently have a hinting system, but [detecting, tracking and leveraging ordering metadata](https://github.com/duckdblabs/duckdb-internal/issues/3741) is something we are looking into.
